top_issues.description: The excerpt ends before the harvest begins. The book's central promise — the harvest as crucible for family reconciliation — is entirely in setup. If the harvest chapters don't match the quality of the setup, the book will feel front-loaded.

Tobe is the least psychologically developed of the three siblings. His guilt about the pump money is powerful when revealed, but his interiority between scenes is thin — he functions more as a structural pivot than a fully inhabited consciousness.

The mechanics of Margo's fraud are slightly elided. A 2019 Medicare power of attorney being used to execute a real estate bridge loan in 2024 requires more legal scaffolding than the text provides. A careful reader may flag this as implausible.

The vote to make wine (Chapter 7) resolves the sell-vs-make conflict very quickly after the dinner table confrontation. The emotional weight of the father revelation and the practical weight of the financial decision are handled in the same breath, which slightly undercuts both.

The list chapter, while well-executed, temporarily flattens the emotional stakes into logistics. The reader is briefly in a planning document rather than a drama. This is a structural necessity but risks losing readers who came for the family conflict.

summary: This is an exceptionally well-constructed ensemble family drama with a distinctive prose voice, a dense and elegant causal architecture, and characters whose psychological specificity feels genuinely novelistic. The setup is nearly flawless — the will's condition, the competing family myths, the secret lien, and Sixto's omniscient silence are all deployed with precision and restraint. The book's primary risk is that it is entirely in setup at the point the excerpt ends, and the harvest chapters — the book's actual promise — remain unwritten and unproven.
